newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Protesters retreat as Zimbabwe orders ban.
newsitem.headline: Protesters retreat as Zimbabwe orders ban.

text.p: Guerrilla war veterans protesting in the Zimbabwean capital Harare retreated on Wednesday in the face of a government ban on demonstrations to prevent embarrassment at the current African/American summit.
Dozens of riot police ringed the Harare International Conference Centre in a show of force after some 300 former guerrillas on Tuesday invaded it in a protest over war pensions.

Home Affairs Minister Dumiso Dabengwa announced the ban on Tuesday night, saying it would last two weeks and affect "all demonstrations that disrupt the smooth flow of traffic and inconvenience the public".

The four-day fourth African/African-American Summit, which began on Tuesday, and is being attended by about 20 African leaders and chief executives from top U.S. companies , is aimed at drumming up investment, trade and general economic support for Africa -- the world's poorest continent.

U.S. civil rights leader Jesse Jackson, co-leader of the American delegation representing President Bill Clinton at the four-day summit, voiced concern over the ban announced overnight but said he would not be drawn into domestic issues.

Instead, he praised Zimbabwe as a democracy and said President Robert Mugabe's leadership in securing stable black-white co-existence since independence in 1980 was a factor in enabling South Africa's former white rulers to hand over power.

"I think it would be a mistake to attempt to micro-analyse a particular issue like this. Zimbabwe is a democracy with a stable government, independent judiciary and a growing economy," he told reporters.
"I am a human rights leader and I am concerned (at the ban), but I have to look at this matter in macro terms... these protests are not defining Zimbabwe as we know it."
Jackson, who on Tuesday lauded the protests as a sign of freedom of expression in Zimbabwe, declined to say if he saw the ban as a backward step for democracy.
"Sometimes in a democracy you take hits, but there is no sign that the democratic institutions in Zimbabwe are weak," he said.

A Reuters reporter saw about 100 war veterans around the headquarters of Zimbabwe's ruling ZANU-PF party and a few others in the conference grounds, but no sign that they would invade the nearby conference centre for a second day.
Their spokesman, Mike Moyo, was non-comittal on what they would now do in the face of the ban, saying only: "All we want is to see our patron."
Mugabe is patron of the Zimbabwe National Liberation War Veterans Association, the representative body of thousands of guerrillas he led during a seven-year independence war in the 1970s.
The veterans have been demanding to see Mugabe for weeks to discuss a war victim compensation fund the government suspended in March to facilitate investigations into allegations of massive fraud.
